summary: A 1970 note giving BBN's comments on the host-host protocol proposed in RFC 33, which it updates. BBN was the company building the network's message processors.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 47 records Bill Crowther's comments on the host protocol in RFC 33. He argues that IMP buffers should absorb short traffic surges, while hosts should buffer messages for their users.

questions: why imp buffers must be empty
what did bbn say about imp buffers
subtitle: BBN's comments on buffering and traffic flow in the proposed host protocol.

tldr.problem: RFC 33, in Bill Crowther's view, overestimated how long messages waited in IMP buffers and misunderstood their role in handling traffic surges.
tldr.mechanism: Crowther explains that IMP buffers are minimal and argues that hosts, rather than IMPs, should handle user-message buffering.
tldr.outcome: RFC 47 updates RFC 33 and records BBN's comments on the draft host protocol.

facts.label: Messages allowed per host in an IMP

today: RFC 47 updates RFC 33. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that updates or replaces RFC 47.

sections.title: What IMP Buffers Are For
sections.content:
Crowther says RFC 33 treats the network as if messages wait in buffers for substantial periods. He offers a different model: messages emerge soon after being inserted, with most delay caused by phone-line hardware.

In his account, IMP buffering is minimal and serves error control and momentary traffic surges. The RFNM mechanism suspends new input until a host accepts a message.
sections.plainLanguage: Crowther describes IMPs as passing messages through quickly. Their limited buffers are there for temporary surges, not to store a queue of user messages.

sections.title: The Disagreement About Links and Traffic
sections.content:
Crowther disputes RFC 33's suggestion that users would not use multiple links to obtain greater bandwidth. He says wider bandwidth is a primary purpose of links and that BBN's difficulty is an imbalance between input and output, not the use of multiple links.

He also distinguishes random single-message traffic from non-random coincidences and bursts. He says BBN has special precautions for bursts and that the host protocol should account for different kinds of users.
sections.plainLanguage: Crowther says multiple links can provide wider bandwidth. He identifies an imbalance between incoming and outgoing traffic, especially bursts, as the concern for IMPs.

sections.title: Why Buffering Belongs at the Host
sections.content:
Crowther says a host should accept a message promptly when an IMP has more than one waiting, because otherwise the IMP has less capacity for a surge. At the time described, an IMP allowed three full-length messages for a host before backing traffic up in the network.

He argues that buffering is a host function because needs differ among time-sharing systems and host operating systems can share memory. He concludes that IMP buffers must be empty to be available for their intended surge-handling purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: The host should manage messages for its own users. That leaves the IMP's small buffer space available for brief traffic surges.

references.text: NWG/RFC 33, the Host Protocol paper that BBN comments on.
